posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Developing only 5 seconds? That’s pretty short! When I shoot the equivaent to the Slavich PFG-03C, the Sphere-S GEO-3, I standardize at 30 seconds development time and vary the exposure time to make a decent density. [http://nlutie.com/ewesly/HnEPortfolio/ColdJD4.html](http://nlutie.com/ewesly/HnEPortfolio/ColdJD4.html)

So if you go this route, you will probably decrease your exposure, which helps out for stability, as it looks like in your second photo you might be having some plate movement; the bottom doesn’t move enough, but as you get up higher the plate is moving more, and you lose the image. Think of a door closing; the side nearest the hinge doesn’t move as much as the edge opposite the hinge. So check your plateholder for stability. 

The white patchy haze is caused by too much density, so you could stand to spread out your reference beam a little more to make it even all over the late. Do you have a spatial filter yet? If you are doing this type of hologram, it would be a good idea.

Slavich is not noted for their coating quality, so the spots could be there courtesy of the factory. Developing a fogged plate, with no holo exposure, might show these same spots.

For something like this material, with its super fine grains, it is prone to fog from the oxygen in the atmosphere! This is why the Ultimate plates come vacuum-packed. Some of your brightness problems may be arising from the plates developing some fog density on top of the holographic exposure. Cut off a chunk of a plate and develop it and see if it turns dark with no exposure to light. If it does, then use a rehalogenating bleach to erase the fog. [http://nlutie.com/ewesly/Publications/recycle.pdf](http://nlutie.com/ewesly/Publications/recycle.pdf)

Whatever they use for gelatin in both the Slavich and Sphere-S plates does take a long time to dry. If you use alcohol baths after the wash then it will dry quicker. I haven’t tried it, but Stas from Geola says it’s a must. [http://materials.geola.lt/index.php/holomaterials/color](http://materials.geola.lt/index.php/holomaterials/color) It does make sense, but I just let the GEO-3 dry overnight.

It is normal to see a “spurious transmission image” (either Jeff Blyth or Graham Saxby dubbed it that in a holosphere article). A transmission image is formed simultaneously with the reflection image, with the reflection of the reflection hologram’s reference from the back of the plate providing the reference for the transmission image.

Looks like you are on the right track, the color of the doll’s head looks pretty real, sometimes I wonder if the blue component is necessary for some scenes.

Keep up the good work, you are almost there!

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
I am not so sure why Geola would list SM-6 as a developer for CW work, as it was discovered while doing research on pulsed holography. See [http://holowiki.nss.rpi.edu/wiki/index. ... lae_/_SM-6](http://holowiki.nss.rpi.edu/wiki/index.php/Ewesly_/_Holographic_Formulae_/_SM-6), especially down at the bottom the links to the Sources. It is a very high-energy developer, and great attention must be paid to control of fog. And I have not tried it with the Slavich PFG-03C as they recommend.

I got great results on Sphere-S GEO-3, which seems to be available from Geola again. From what I have heard, Sphere-S is a spin-off from Slavich, headed by a character named Suzanov, (I think that might be the correct spelling, hopefully Valery can give us more details), who was in charge of the holographic products at Slavich. The samples I received were well-coated, not like the PFG, and responded well to the cold water processing regime.

The cold water processing link to my grad school web site (nlutie.com/ewesly) seems to be down for now, maybe John Fisher can post it on the Wiki portion of this site. (“There is a server resource overage report open for this account in the User area.” Something seems to use up a quota every month, the site goes down, then comes back up at the beginning of the new billing period. I can’t complain too much as I had graduated from National Louis University 3 years ago, and they haven’t closed me down and are hosting my site for free. I guess I have to find my own host sooner than later!)

The cold water pre-soak, and low processing temperature were the innovations of Tung Jeong. The grand finale to his lectures would be the recording of a Denisyuk hologram in front of a group of people. The cold water pre-soak was his was way of hardening the gelatin without using formaldehyde. I finally tried it on GEO-3 plates, and used the JD-4 developer, (and see the holowiki for my discussion of that formula), and the reasons I went to that recipe for the GEO-3 plates was that TJ was using it on the PFG-03M, and that formula, which had been invented by Jeff Blyth for the Hologaphic Recording Technology (now Colour Holographics) worked very well on their BB-640 and 520 plates, which I figured were close enough to the GEO-3.

The bleach that I had used in those trials was 2 g Potassium Dichromate, 2 mL Sulfuric Acid (or 6 g Sodium Bisulfate), and 30 g Potassium Bromide, not the PBU Amidol, which I have never used. It was surprising how well it worked! Geola probably recommends that bleach on Hans’s recommendations to them, as he does takes credit for the use of the formaldehyde pre-hardener.

I only shot one chunk of PFG-03C for my paper for the ISDH at MIT, at 458 nm, so that is the extent of my experience with that material. But it was processed in the cold water regime, and not too bad, but then again, it is hard to judge blue holograms. One of these days I will use it in the red or green!

And maybe even use the film that Valery had sent me years ago! I am sorry to say I had received a sample from him quite a few years ago, and have not had the opportunity to try it! Valery, please do not be upset with me, there is only so much I can do!

I saw some stereograms on Valery’s material that Jeff Weil brought to my house, and they are of the high quality one would expect from these ultra-fine grain emulsions!

So that is all I know about all these things! Hope this helps!

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
Perhaps the increase in hardness is a result of nucleation by impurities in the gelatin. Perhaps the coldness of the water causes polymerisation with impurities in the gelatin (or in the gelatin itself), because of the lower KE and so the higher the capture probability and so the higher the probability of polymerisation (especially considering the polarity of the water molecule) while the warmer water has a higher KE and so lowering the capture cross section.

Of course the another explanation is that lower the temperature of the water, the more the precipitation of impurities. Some of these impurities may polymerise with the gelatin molecule. For example certain chromium salts are known gelatin hardeners. Thus, if these substances were dissolved in the water, then decreasing the temperature of the water would precipitate them into the gelatin matrix. The presence of the gelatin may act as a catalyst for the precipitation.

The internet is a perfect crucible for experimental verification! If people across the globe measure the increase in hardness of gelatin and find a consistent result, it shows that the culprit is the water itself, since correlation of impurities in water on a global scale has a very low probability. However, if there is a variation of hardness across the globe for the same temperature, then I would suspect dissolved substances in the water.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
Regarding cold water treatment:

I don't think it has anything to do with gelatin hardening.

A cold water pre-soak simply provides the means for even development throughout the emulsion - particularly if the developer temperature has to be kept low (to prevent gelatin damage as in the PFG-03 case).

As for the JD-4 hardening action, it's probably due to its metol part. The oxidized metol seems to form a PBQ-like agent that can crosslink gelatin (as can be seen by the "PBU-metol" bleach).

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
> **Joe Farina:** Any other ideas?

1. Place the processing tray inside a larger tray. Add a mixture of ice and water to the larger tray. This ensures the temp of the processing tray is 0 C (=/- delta T). Then place a thermostat such that it's set to some temp between 0 and room temp.

2. Place alcohol in the larger tray with a fan blowing onto the alcohol. The speed of the fan is regulated by some temperature dependent device, such as a thermistor.

3. Peltier chip?

4. Connect a high pressure hose to your water supply. Force large amounts of water through a very narrow nozzle. Spray processing tray.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
It doesn't have to be that close to freezing cold! For the cold pre-soak, I just use the cold water that comes out of the pipes, typical Chicago water temperature from the cold tap is in the 45 to 50 degree Fahrenheit range, 7 to 10 Centigrade, and that is fine for the pre-soak.

Maintaining the 65F (18C) is done simply by putting the tray inside of a larger tray with cold tap water, or even ice cubes. These are all old school photography darkroom operating procedures.

I have stainless steel developing tanks that sit in a bigger bowl with the cold water when developing 4 by 5's. No need for refrigerators, but what is great is an automatic temperature regulating faucet. Then the darkroom sink can be filled with the temperature stabilized water and the trays sit inside that.

Whatever the mechanism for the success of this processing tip, it is essential for these materials, just try processing without it, and you will see color blotches or the emulsion come clean off the plate! Pre-soaks in photographic processing have been around forever, and it does promote even development, but is not necessary for all emulsions. Photo paper usually doesn't need it, sometimes it does help film. But the ultra-fine grain holo products do respond nicely to this regime!

posts.author: Sphere-S
posts.content_md:
Hello everybody, 

We have not visited the forum for ages since nobody is interested in photomaterials. As we understand GEO-3 plates are Sphere-S HP-C plates which we produced last time in 2010. For last 2 years we have been producing plates of big size for our great friends from Kiev and Minsk. 

For last 8 months holographic market is being revived. We produced a big quantity of color holographic film and several types of plates for different purposes. Our photomaterials cannot be compared with Slavich materials since they are not similar. We read at the forum discussion that Sphere-S materials are compared with Slavich ones. Each consumer needs its own photomaterial since all consumers have different laser capacity, different possibilities of chemical processing, etc. So each consumer wishes to get such a material which is ideal for his working conditions. Some consumers who have high energy lasers may expose less sensitive material which will be strongly hardened and can be processed and dried without alcohols. 

Other consumers have not such possibilities and they need more sensitive material, 5 - 6 times more sensitive. So they have to get non-hardened material since during hardening light sensitivity of photomaterial strongly drops. But they may use lasers with less capacity. Development in the second case is complicated by alcohol drying and preliminary hardening. We show just 2 samples of different demands to material which can be suitable for 2 types of consumers. One needs processing without alcohol but with loss of light sensitivity, the second needs high light sensitivity with more difficult processing. There can be a number of samples since each consumer needs photomaterial suitable for his possibilities. 

Currently we may produce different photomaterials with different characteristics from red sensitive material up to color material for pulse laser which is our main product. We do not propose our plates and films to be sold in the market since orders are quite small and delivery cost will be higher than photomaterial cost. 

Our proposal which will be profitable for both sides is to find a person who will collect the orders from you, combine them and place at Sphere. Please, be informed , delivery cost will be paid by customers. 

P.S. . We read at the forum about the problems with PFG-03M processing . Our experience is that the plates which are analogous to PFG-03M are not intended to be bleached. You will not get any advantages in efficiency after bleaching this material. To my mind SM-6 developer and PBU-amidol (metol) bleacher usage is better than your method. If you want to get anything homogeneous temperature of processing solutions should be 14- 18 degrees C. All processing solutions and alcohols in which a hologram is dried should have this temperature. 

Another variant of the better drying is hardening in 2% solution of formaline from 2 up to 4 minutes. Then processing in SM6 from 2 up to 3 minutes, then washing in filtered water, then bleaching for 5 minutes or up to complete bleaching, then washing in filtered water. Your problems with spots, fogging are not caused just by exposure, but also by high temperature of processing of non-hardened photomaterial. You need decrease temperature of processing if you dry in alcohol. To understand the processes of shooting, processing, drying Sergey Vorobjev wrote special “Holography Lessons”. They include the most simple and easy to understand process descriptions. You may find it in Internet.

posts.author: Holomark
posts.content_md:
After using the last of the PFG03C plates in stock and testing a variety of different exposure levels and developing techniques, the plates with the least/no obstructive whiteness were those that were processed with the emulsion side DOWN. I know Ed mentions this in the processing regime (dont recall if it was this product or another), and it seems to allow something to fall out instead of building up on top of the emulsion. Lots of fresh water also a must (I was a bit skimpy with fresh rinse water due to drought and believe this may have contributed to the problem)

In the end, while I got some holograms with these plates I was not overly impressed with the brightness level I achieved. I don't seem to be hitting the real sweet spot an not really sure if theissue is development or exposure. While I was able to get two colors with both single beam and split beam systems, but never really got everything to work right at the sam time. Never really got the sensitivity/exposure curves for the to colors refined as I would like - I seem to have gotten the best results with 623 at 3000 uW and 532 at 8000 uW.
